subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]
passage: On the whiteboard in the Chennai office, Rehana wrote: "Users leave within a week." Kunal, the product lead, tapped the marker. "Why?" "They drop off during setup." "Why?" "The onboarding asks for too much." "Why does it ask for so much?" "Because the school's admin wants all the data before anything starts." "Why does the admin decide that?" "Because the admin bought it." "And why does that matter?" Rehana stopped. "Because the teachers who use it never chose it, never paid for it, and were never asked." They stared at the fifth answer. "So it isn't the onboarding," said Rehana. "It's who we thought our user was." Kunal wrote a new line at the bottom: "Talk to the people who pay."

qa.q: What did Rehana first write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: Rehana wrote, "Users leave within a week."

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Rehana stopped at the fifth question?
qa.a: Rehana was struck and realising something uncomfortable, that the problem was not the onboarding.

qa.q: What could the team do next?
qa.a: They could interview the school admins who decide and pay, as well as the teachers, and rethink who the product is for.

qa.q: How might the teachers have seen the app?
qa.a: The teachers may have seen it as something imposed on them, which they never chose or paid for.

grounding: Rehana and Kunal ask why five times about users leaving and find the users were never the ones who paid or decided.

"Seventy percent gone in the first week," Indu said, staring at the chart. "Why?"
"Because they don't finish setting up," Keerthana said.
"Why don't they finish setting up?"
"The setup asks for the tax number and bank details on screen two."
"Why would that stop them?"
Keerthana scrolled through the signup list. "Because... they don't have them. Look at the job titles. Waiters. Cashiers. Kitchen staff."
"Why are cashiers signing up for an expense tool?"
"Because we advertised in restaurant staff groups. They liked the idea. But they can't pay for it and they can't decide."
"So why are they leaving?"
"Because they were never our customers. The owners are."
Indu leaned back. "We've spent three months fixing the setup screens for people who were never going to buy."

qa.q: What share of users left in the first week?
How did Indu feel on realising they had spent three months on the wrong people?
qa.a: Indu felt dismayed and a bit deflated, but also clearer about the real problem.

qa.q: What should the team try next?
qa.a: Talk directly to restaurant owners, who pay and decide, and design the setup around them.

qa.q: How might the waiters and cashiers see the app?
qa.a: They liked the idea but got stuck on details they didn't have, so for them it was a dead end.

grounding: It shows a team asking why repeatedly about users leaving in the first week, moving from a clumsy setup flow to finding the users never paid or decided.

subtype: Approach: five whys on the churn numbers [Thinking]
passage:
Our study-planner app had a leak we couldn't plug: most students deleted it within six days. Anjali and I had redesigned the first screens three times. Nothing moved.
One night Anjali said, "Lokesh, let's just keep asking why." So we did, on the whiteboard.
Why do they leave? They stop opening it after day two.
Why? The reminders feel like nagging.
Why does it feel like nagging? They didn't choose it; their parents installed it.
Why did the parents install it? The school told them to.
Why does that matter? Because the students were never the ones deciding. Parents and teachers were.
I remember staring at that last line. We had been designing for teenagers who never wanted the app. We needed to talk to the people who actually chose it and paid for it.

qa.q: Within how many days did most students delete the app?
What was Lokesh feeling while staring at the last line?
qa.a: Lokesh felt stunned and a little foolish, realising they had been designing for the wrong people.

qa.q: What should Lokesh and Anjali do next?
qa.a: Interview parents and teachers, the real deciders, about what they want a planner to do.

qa.q: How might the students have experienced the app?
qa.a: They felt nagged by an app they hadn't chosen, which is why they stopped opening it after day two.

grounding: It shows a team asking why five times about users quitting in the first week and discovering the users were never the people who paid or decided.
